cards.title: Low-dimensional parallel convex-optimization lower bounds
cards.formal: In the low-dimensional regime, is the high-probability K-parallel local-oracle complexity of convex optimization at least Ω(d·ln(1/ε)/ln(K/γ)), for the nonsmooth, weakly smooth and smooth settings intended by the source? Here d is dimension, K is the number of simultaneous queries per round, ε is normalized additive optimization accuracy, and γ is the source’s success-confidence parameter. The denominator and d were damaged in the imported excerpt. The conjecture’s joint parameter regime and geometric scope still need specification before it is a fully quantified lower-bound statement.
cards.why: Would quantify the limits of parallel oracle queries when dimension is too small for existing high-dimensional hard instances, a regime where parallel speedups can actually occur.
cards.status_note: Read the confidence definition and final formula in the conference paper, the revised journal discussion, and the 2025 full lower-bound section. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not establish the historical low-dimensional conjecture with a complete joint regime. Its confidence and geometry qualifications remain necessary, so it is not certified as a current fully specified theorem target.

cards.review_note: The recovered formula omits a precise joint low-dimensional regime for d,ε,K,γ, which must accompany a uniform Ω bound. The allowed norm geometry and the normalization of the function class are not fixed by the final conjecture sentence. The confidence range also matters: γ is success probability, and the displayed denominator cannot be used without qualification all the way to K=1,γ→1. The 2020 journal conclusion changes the surrounding discussion and does not supply these missing quantifiers. No arbitrary Euclidean specialization or parameter range is certified here.

category_assignment.reason: The lower bound concerns adaptive rounds of parallel oracle queries in convex optimization, with the parallel access model central.

importance.reason: A general limit on useful parallelism in low-dimensional convex optimization, sensitive to geometry and confidence. Existing score retained.

sentences: A parallel convex optimizer queries at most K points before seeing that round’s answers.
The source conjectures a round lower bound proportional to d·ln(1/ε)/ln(K/γ) in low dimensions.
Here γ is success confidence, and ε measures the additive gap from the optimum.
The journal revision and recent high-dimensional smooth results address related but distinct regimes.
The intended geometry, scale normalization and joint parameter range remain necessary to complete the conjecture.

cards.definitions: The source considers a finite-dimensional normed space E=Rᵈ, a known closed convex feasible set X, and an unknown convex objective f:E→R from a class F. The goal is a point x∈X with f(x)−inf_{y∈X}f(y)≤ε. Its geometric settings include unit balls B_p^d={x:‖x‖ₚ≤1}, where ‖x‖ₚ=(Σᵢ|xᵢ|ᵖ)^{1/p} for finite p≥1 and ‖x‖∞=maxᵢ|xᵢ|. A local oracle O satisfies O_f(x)=O_g(x) whenever f and g agree on a neighborhood of x. Gradient or suitable local subgradient information is a special case; exact internal arithmetic is not the resource counted. In a K-parallel algorithm, a whole batch of at most K query points is chosen before any answer in that batch is seen. Later batches may depend on all previous answers. Cost is rounds of such batches, not the total K times that number of queries. For an objective class F, fixed oracle O and deterministic K-parallel algorithm A, let T(A,f,ε) be the number of rounds until A finds an ε-accurate feasible point. The source defines C_HP^γ=sup_D inf_A inf{τ: Pr_{f drawn from D}[T(A,f,ε)≤τ]≥γ}, where D ranges over probability distributions supported on F and 0<γ<1. Thus a hard distribution is chosen before the deterministic algorithm, which may know it; the distributional lower bound also constrains randomized algorithms. In this convention γ is the required success probability. Nonsmooth classes include Lipschitz convex functions, |f(x)−f(y)|≤L‖x−y‖. Weakly smooth classes have Hölder-continuous gradients, ‖∇f(x)−∇f(y)‖_*≤μ‖x−y‖^κ for 0<κ<1; κ=1 gives Lipschitz-continuous gradients. The dual norm is ‖v‖_*=sup_{‖x‖≤1}|⟨v,x⟩|. The source also uses a nonsmooth normalization through bounded variation of subgradients. Bounds in ln(1/ε) presuppose fixing these scales and the radius of X. Low-dimensional means a regime outside the dimension requirements of the source’s high-dimensional lower bounds, but that phrase alone does not prescribe a numerical relation among the parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: For precisely specified objective classes, geometries and a joint range of d,K,ε,γ, prove the displayed lower bound with constants uniform over that range, or refute it by a valid oracle algorithm violating the bound there. A result that assumes dimension polynomially large in inverse accuracy, treats only deterministic worst-case complexity, or uses total queries instead of rounds does not automatically establish this high-probability low-dimensional claim. The omitted parameter and class conventions must be resolved before this is a complete benchmark proposition.

context_blocks.title: The confidence convention changes the formula
context_blocks.text: The source’s quantile definition requires success probability at least γ. Substituting a failure probability would reverse the meaning of the parameter in ln(K/γ). The imported excerpt also detached d from its numerator.

context_blocks.title: The historical nonsmooth box bound is weaker
context_blocks.text: The conference conclusion compares Nemirovski’s deterministic ℓ∞ lower bound Ω((d/ln(dK))^{1/3}ln(1/ε)) with a desired linear dependence on d up to a logarithm. Its randomized argument recovers a related scale only for constant accuracy.

context_blocks.title: The journal discussion is more qualified
context_blocks.text: The 2020 version discusses known low-dimensional Euclidean parallel speedups and asks about other geometries. Its conclusion does not reproduce the conference’s smooth-and-nonsmooth confidence formula with full quantifiers.

context_blocks.title: The recent resolution concerns high dimensions
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper improves smooth parallel lower bounds, including the previously weaker ℓ₁ exponent, under sufficiently large dimension. Its abstract’s statement that it resolves an open parallel-optimization question does not identify this low-dimensional conjecture as solved.

cards.context:
The source’s quantile definition requires success probability at least γ. Substituting a failure probability would reverse the meaning of the parameter in ln(K/γ). The imported excerpt also detached d from its numerator.

The conference conclusion compares Nemirovski’s deterministic ℓ∞ lower bound Ω((d/ln(dK))^{1/3}ln(1/ε)) with a desired linear dependence on d up to a logarithm. Its randomized argument recovers a related scale only for constant accuracy.

The 2020 version discusses known low-dimensional Euclidean parallel speedups and asks about other geometries. Its conclusion does not reproduce the conference’s smooth-and-nonsmooth confidence formula with full quantifiers.

The 2025 paper improves smooth parallel lower bounds, including the previously weaker ℓ₁ exponent, under sufficiently large dimension. Its abstract’s statement that it resolves an open parallel-optimization question does not identify this low-dimensional conjecture as solved.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
